stem: For a hypothetical day's 100 tonnes of waste, a town can feasibly reuse 20 tonnes and recycle 30 different tonnes. Of the remaining 50, exactly 30 are compostable, but today's composting capacity is 20 tonnes; no other recovery is feasible. Under RA 9003's recovery-and-residual planning approach, which plan uses all today's feasible recovery and provides sufficient suitable disposal capacity? These capacities are supplied assumptions, not statutory quotas.

choices.text: Recover 50 tonnes and provide disposal for 50 tonnes.
Recover 70 tonnes and provide disposal for 30 tonnes.
Recover 80 tonnes and provide disposal for 20 tonnes.
Recover 70 tonnes and provide disposal for 20 tonnes.

explanation: Feasible recovery is 20 reuse + 30 recycling + min(30 compostable,20 capacity) = 70 tonnes. Residuals are 100−70=30, including ten compostable tonnes beyond today's feasible capacity. Eighty recovered ignores capacity; 20 disposal misses residuals; recovering only 50 omits feasible composting. Section 16 calls for feasible recovery and appropriate residual disposal, not these hypothetical numerical weights.

stem: A Philippine government office abroad handles a nonbusiness application. Adviser A charges only for explaining published requirements and has no access to staff. Intermediary B charges to speed completion using personal access to agency staff. Under RA 11032's coverage and fixer definitions, which classification follows from these facts alone?

choices.text: The service is excluded because it is abroad; B nevertheless fits the access-and-gain description.
The service is excluded because it is nonbusiness; neither A nor B can fit the fixer definition.
The service is covered; B fits the fixer definition, while the facts do not establish that A does.
The service is covered; both A and B fit the fixer definition merely because each charges.

explanation: Amended Section 3 covers Philippine government services abroad and nonbusiness transactions. Section 4(e) requires the specified access and speedy facilitation for gain, not payment for any advice. B meets that description; the facts about A do not. Coverage and the distinction between paid advice and fixing must both be retained.

stem: Under RA 11032's definitions, Service A involves a long packet but only routine ministerial checking; Service B has a short packet but requires specialised technical evaluation. Both collect prescribed fees, yet their Citizen's Charter entries omit fee amounts. Which assessment addresses both classifications and both omissions?

choices.text: A is highly technical and B simple; only B's entry must disclose its applicable fee amount.
A is simple and B highly technical; both entries must disclose the applicable fee amounts.
A is simple and B highly technical; only B's entry must disclose its applicable fee amount.
A is highly technical and B simple; both entries must disclose the applicable fee amounts.

explanation: Amended Sections 4(g),(m) classify the work, not packet length: A is ministerial/simple; B requires specialised evaluation. Section 6(f)'s fee disclosure applies here because both services collect fees. Neither a correct classification nor a short form excuses an applicable fee omission.
